entry.title: Select Initial assessment or After treatment
entry.scope: The phase is a review context, not a clinical normal finding. Initial severity/ECG/dialysis assessment and post-treatment insulin/response surveillance remain separate.

fields.label: Review phase
fields.essential: Select Initial assessment or After treatment. No phase is a clinical finding, and it does not expose either treatment branch.

fields.label: Airway, breathing, circulation or consciousness compromised?
fields.essential: Airway, breathing, circulation or consciousness compromise takes priority; do not wait to finish the assessment.

fields.label: Current credible potassium result (mmol/L)
fields.essential: K 5.5–5.9, 6.0–6.4 and ≥6.5 mmol/L are distinct reviewed bands. Unknown is not a non-hyperkalemic result.

fields.label: ECG changes attributed to hyperkalemia?
fields.essential: Attribute ECG changes clinically. A normal reviewed ECG does not reduce the urgency of severe hyperkalemia.

fields.label: Clinically unwell or a rapid potassium rise anticipated?
Does the patient receive maintenance hemodialysis?

stages.title: Assess & monitor
stages.empty: Review ECG, sample, trend and causes.

stages.title: Protect the heart
stages.empty: Review ECG to assess the need for IV calcium.

stages.title: Shift potassium
stages.empty: Select a credible K value to assess lowering therapy.

stages.title: Remove potassium
stages.empty: Review causes and kidney function; removal depends on severity.

stages.title: Reassess
stages.empty: Set the next K check from severity and treatment.

quickReference.summary: Prioritize clinical stability, potassium severity, ECG findings and dialysis context; treatment and reassessment run in parallel.
recognition: Review the potassium value, sample quality/hemolysis, renal function, acid-base state, glucose, medications, intake, and recent potassium trend.
Obtain or review an ECG promptly for clinically significant hyperkalemia; a reassuring ECG does not exclude risk.
Treat a dangerous presentation without waiting for a repeat result when the clinical picture and initial value are credible.
redFlags: Compromised airway, breathing, circulation or consciousness; K ≥6.5 mmol/L; hyperkalemic ECG changes; or rapidly rising potassium/clinical illness.
Maintenance hemodialysis with K ≥6.5 mmol/L, treatment-resistant hyperkalemia, or persistent/recurrent potassium elevation after treatment.
Unknown stability, potassium, ECG or hemodialysis status does not establish a lower-risk route.

steps.text: UKKA 16.2a suggests IV calcium for hyperkalemia with ECG changes (grade 2C, updated July 2026). Use calcium chloride in arrest/peri-arrest and calcium gluconate otherwise. Calcium protects the heart temporarily but does not lower potassium.

UKKA recommends insulin/glucose for K ≥6.5 mmol/L and suggests it for K 6.0–6.4 mmol/L. Salbutamol is an adjunct, not monotherapy for severe hyperkalemia. Baseline glucose and post-treatment glucose surveillance are essential.

UKKA recommends sodium zirconium cyclosilicate in severe hyperkalemia and suggests considering it in moderate hyperkalemia; patiromer is an option at K ≥6.0. Severe hyperkalemia in maintenance-hemodialysis patients requires urgent dialysis. Binders do not replace immediate stabilization. IV bicarbonate and calcium resonium are not routine acute treatments.

monitoring: UK Kidney Association suggests potassium checks at least 1, 2, 4, 6, and 24 hours after identifying and treating moderate or severe hyperkalemia.
After insulin/glucose, use timed glucose surveillance through 6 hours because delayed hypoglycemia can occur.
Document whether each intervention stabilizes, shifts, or removes potassium so temporary improvement is not mistaken for definitive control.

Local products, concentrations, pump settings, nutrition plans, prescription authority and order-set reconciliation remain local-policy work. The general-admission glucometer resource is not a hypoglycaemia set and does not replace the JBDS timing.
The TPN option means oral intake is not permitted. Select “Oral permitted” if oral rescue is actually available; the engine otherwise asks for a parenteral route.
The 4.0–6.0 mmol/L band is individualised prevention guidance, not an automatic rescue regimen.

The rescue phase is an assessment state, not a medication-administration record, dose counter, timestamp, or authorization. Unknown phase, nutrition or safety keeps urgent clinician review explicit rather than assuming an initial or repeat dose.

entry.text: JBDS inpatient rescue threshold · glucose below 4.0 mmol/L (about 72 mg/dL).
entry.scope: Adults aged 16+ with diabetes; pregnancy and non-diabetic hypoglycaemia need a separate pathway.

fields.label: Rescue phase / current response?
fields.help: Glucose remains the current measured result. JBDS recovery wording requires glucose above 4.0 mmol/L and clinical recovery; do not select recovery while the current result is below 4.0 mmol/L or repeat an initial rescue while a recheck is still due.

fields.label: Nutrition route
options: Enteral feed route in use and usable

quickReference.summary: JBDS adult inpatient pathway: below 4.0 mmol/L is the treatment threshold. Choose a safe route, recheck to recovery, then prevent recurrence.
recognition: Treat any glucose below 4.0 mmol/L in this source population, with or without symptoms.
4.0–6.0 mmol/L is “looming” hypoglycaemia: review risk and individualise; it is not the same rescue threshold.
Check ABCDE and capillary glucose promptly; do not delay urgent treatment when a seizure or unsafe state prevents immediate measurement.
redFlags: Unconsciousness, seizure, very aggressive behaviour, unsafe swallow, or persistent altered consciousness.
Glucose still below 4.0 mmol/L after 30–45 minutes or 3 rescue cycles.
Severe or recurrent event, long-acting insulin or sulfonylurea exposure, renal impairment, interrupted nutrition, or prolonged fasting.

steps.text: ABCDE; stop an active insulin infusion during confirmed hypoglycaemia.
15–20 g rapid carbohydrate; recheck in 10–15 min; no more than 3 cycles.
IV: 20% glucose 100 mL or 10% glucose 200 mL over 15 min. No IV: glucagon 1 mg IM while obtaining access.
steps.dosingNote: Confirm local product, concentration and pump setting.

steps.text: When above 4.0 mmol/L and recovered: 20 g longer-acting carbohydrate; 40 g after glucagon. NPO requires a separate IV-glucose bridge plan.
Review active treatment, meals/feeds and illness. Do not automatically omit the next insulin dose; continue regular glucose monitoring 24–48 h.

monitoring: Oral, buccal or enteral rescue: recheck capillary glucose after 10–15 minutes; maximum 3 treatment cycles before escalation.
IV glucose or IM glucagon: recheck capillary glucose after 10 minutes.
After sulfonylurea or long-acting insulin, recurrence may persist 24–36 hours; this adds prolonged risk to the general 24–48-hour monitoring plan.

entry.title: Acute breathlessness or hypoxaemia
entry.scope: Assess ABC/critical illness, hypercapnia risk, oxygenation trajectory and ventilation separately. Unknown criticality or risk does not infer an oxygen target.

fields.label: Critical illness or severe ABC compromise?
fields.essential: Critical illness or severe ABC compromise takes priority over target selection; do not delay emergency support.

fields.label: Known risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure?
fields.essential: A known hypercapnia risk requires an explicit non-critical assessment before the 88–92% initial target branch appears.

fields.label: Below target, falls ≥3%, or support increasing?
Drowsiness, fatigue, poor effort, or CO₂/acidosis concern?

stages.title: Stabilize
stages.empty: No critical illness entered.

stages.title: Set target
stages.empty: Critical-illness target appears above, or assess critical illness first.

stages.title: Assess ventilation
stages.empty: No additional gas trigger entered.

quickReference.summary: Set a documented oxygen target, identify ventilatory failure early, and treat the likely cause in parallel.
recognition: Record SpO₂ with the device, flow or FiO₂; verify the waveform.
Pulse oximetry does not show CO₂, pH, oxygen content or the underlying cause.
redFlags: Critical illness, ABC compromise, exhaustion/poor effort, new drowsiness or airway-protection concern.
Target breach, ≥3% saturation fall, increasing oxygen requirement, or suspected CO₂ retention/acidosis.

steps.text: Critical illness: initially aim 94–98% while blood gases and expert assessment are obtained, even with hypercapnia risk. Once critical illness is assessed absent, known hypercapnia risk: 88–92% pending gases; known no risk: 94–98%.
steps.dosingNote: Oxygen is a treatment for hypoxaemia, not breathlessness alone.

steps.text: Obtain blood gases for critical illness, hypercapnia risk, falling saturation, rising oxygen need, drowsiness or suspected acidosis. Record support context and reassess after material change.
Route bronchospasm, pulmonary oedema, anaphylaxis or another likely syndrome to its cause-specific local pathway. Do not configure ventilatory support from this guide.

monitoring: Record saturation, device and flow / FiO₂ with complete observations and after material support changes.
For hypercapnia-risk patients, BTS advises repeat blood gases after 30–60 minutes or earlier deterioration even when the first gas is reassuring.

entry.title: Measured K below 3.5 mmol/L
entry.scope: K at or below 2.5 mmol/L, ECG/rhythm abnormality, paralysis, respiratory failure, or severe weakness are urgent features. Unknown findings are not normal.

fields.label: Potassium · mmol/L
fields.help: Use the current measured potassium. ≤2.5 mmol/L is a severe feature. >2.5 to <3.5 covers every value between those boundaries; ≥3.5 does not trigger hypokalaemia replacement. Unknown is never treated as normal.
fields.essential: Hypokalaemia is measured potassium below 3.5 mmol/L. Potassium at or below 2.5 mmol/L is a severe biochemical feature; unknown is not normal.

fields.label: Urgent ECG / neuromuscular feature?
fields.help: Present/suspected means any ECG abnormality or arrhythmia, paralysis, respiratory failure, or severe weakness. Absent means these urgent features were actively assessed.
fields.essential: Danger: ECG/rhythm abnormality, paralysis, respiratory failure or severe weakness.

fields.label: Oral / GI route safe?
fields.help: Safe/functioning means a safe swallow, a functioning GI tract, and an appropriate available formulation. No includes unsafe swallowing, an unavailable route, or a nonfunctioning GI tract.
fields.essential: A safe oral route requires a safe swallow, functioning GI tract, and an appropriate available formulation.

fields.label: Reduced K clearance / risk?
fields.help: Risk present includes renal impairment, oliguria/anuria, or potassium-retaining treatment such as RAAS inhibition, potassium-sparing diuretics, or NSAIDs. No risk requires active review.

fields.label: Magnesium status?
fields.help: Unknown means magnesium has not been checked. Low captures a documented deficit; not low requires a reviewed result. This finding does not prescribe a magnesium dose or route.

fields.label: Most likely mechanism?
fields.help: Select only a reviewed mechanism: GI loss/poor intake, renal loss/diuretic exposure, or intracellular shift. Unclear means initial review has not established the cause and prompts clinician-owned work-up.

stages.title: Verify & triage
stages.empty: Confirm the potassium result and urgent features.

stages.title: Choose route
stages.empty: A safe route follows verified severity and findings.

stages.title: Safeguard replacement
stages.empty: Review renal clearance and IV controls.

stages.title: Correct contributors
stages.empty: Review magnesium and the mechanism.

stages.title: Recheck response
stages.empty: Set the next potassium and clinical review.

quickReference.summary: Confirm a true low potassium, identify urgent features, choose oral versus supervised IV replacement, correct contributors, and measure the response.
recognition: AAFP defines hypokalaemia as potassium below 3.5 mmol/L; confirm an unexpected result and review its trend.
Urgent features include potassium ≤2.5 mmol/L, ECG/rhythm abnormality, paralysis, respiratory failure, or severe weakness.
Obtain an ECG when hypokalaemia is identified, but an absent ECG change does not exclude clinically important depletion.
redFlags: Arrhythmia, ECG change, syncope/cardiac instability, paralysis, respiratory failure, or severe weakness.
Potassium ≤2.5 mmol/L, rapidly falling potassium, digoxin/cardiac disease context, or inability to take oral treatment.
Oliguria/severe renal impairment, potassium-retaining medicines, uncontrolled loss, hypomagnesaemia, DKA, refeeding, or uncertain route/monitoring context.

steps.text: Confirm the potassium result when appropriate, review trend and obtain ECG. Do not delay urgent clinical response for an arrhythmia, paralysis, respiratory failure or severe weakness.

With K >2.5 mmol/L, no severe features and a functioning safe GI route, oral potassium is preferred. The reviewed ER KCl label lists 40–100 mEq/day divided for treatment, with no more than 40 mEq in one dose.
steps.dosingNote: Product-specific detail: take ER tablets with meals and liquid; swallow whole. Verify the stocked product and renal plan.

steps.role: Use supervised IV only when indicated
steps.text: For severe features, K ≤2.5 mmol/L, or no safe oral route, use a clinician-directed IV pathway. AAFP describes 5–10 mEq IV KCl over 15–30 min with cardiac monitoring for severe symptoms; stable IV replacement is generally up to 10 mEq/hour peripherally.
steps.dosingNote: 20 mEq/hour is a monitored central-access exception in the AAFP review, not a routine ward regimen. Never IV push; verify local product, pump, concentration and line.

steps.text: Check magnesium, renal clearance, medications, ongoing GI/renal loss and transcellular-shift context. Correct documented deficits and causes through the appropriate local protocol.
Set the next potassium, ECG and clinical review with the selected route. AAFP describes 2–4-hour potassium checks during urgent severe-symptom IV treatment; use local timing for other situations.

monitoring: Use cardiac monitoring for severe symptoms and for IV potassium rates at or above 10 mEq/hour in the AAFP review; verify the local high-risk infusion policy.
Monitor potassium and adjust dosing with renal impairment, oliguria, RAAS inhibitors, NSAIDs, or other potassium-retention risk.
Record the actual product, concentration, line, infusion device, response result, ECG/rhythm and continuing losses. A product catalog does not establish a safe prescription.

guides.reviewNotice: The 2014/2022 source contract was reviewed on 15 September 2026. A 2026 ESE–ERA hyponatraemia update was listed, but final recommendation text was not verified; do not describe this guide as current local policy.
guides.guideVersion: Society for Endocrinology severe/moderately severe symptomatic hyponatraemia guidance (2022), European hyponatraemia guideline (2014), and ODS-risk synthesis (2024), as recorded in the prototype review
guides.resourceNotice: Internal hospital resource tables are omitted from this shared edition.
guides.scope: Adult hyponatraemia: symptom-led emergency response and correction safeguards.
reviewLimitations: This is a compact, source-linked adult decision aid, not a local protocol, prescription, sodium calculator, diagnosis engine, order set, or clinical-authority substitute.

It follows the Society for Endocrinology 2022 emergency figure for accepted severe or moderately severe symptomatic hyponatraemia. The 2014 European guideline differs in its moderate-symptom detail; the response branch keeps that difference visible rather than silently combining a continuous-infusion regimen with the 2022 bolus figure.

Symptoms must be clinically attributed. Mild biochemical hyponatraemia with major symptoms is an exceptional causal claim in the European guideline, so the engine retains alternative-cause review and never decides attribution itself.

The 10 mmol/L first-24-hour and 8 mmol/L later-24-hour values are correction limits, not targets or a declaration of safety. Missing serial values never trigger an inferred “no overcorrection” conclusion.

A 2026 ESE–ERA hyponatraemia update is listed publicly, but final publication/recommendation text was not verified in this review. Re-review this config against that publication and local governance before calling the 2014/2022 sources current local policy.
No HIS connection, patient data, order staging, order submission, product-equivalence decision, or local formulary claim is contained in this data layer.

entry.title: Measured Na below 135 mmol/L
entry.scope: Establish tonicity and symptom attribution separately. A non-low sodium does not enter the hyponatraemia mechanism or sodium-raising pathway.

fields.label: Verified serum sodium?
fields.help: European biochemical bands: mild 130 to <135, moderate 125 to <130, profound <125 mmol/L.
fields.essential: Hyponatraemia is measured serum sodium below 135 mmol/L: mild 130 to below 135, moderate 125 to below 130, profound below 125.

fields.label: Urgent symptom class?
fields.help: Severe: vomiting, cardio-respiratory distress, deep somnolence, seizure or coma. Moderately severe: nausea without vomiting, confusion or headache.
fields.essential: Severe: vomiting, cardiorespiratory distress, deep somnolence, seizure or coma. Moderately severe: nausea without vomiting, confusion or headache.

fields.label: Symptoms due to hyponatraemia?
fields.help: Symptoms are non-specific. Accept the causal relation only after clinical assessment, particularly when sodium is mildly low.
fields.essential: Symptoms are non-specific. Accept a hyponatraemia causal relation only after clinical assessment, especially when sodium is mildly low.

fields.label: Documented time course?
fields.help: Acute is documented <48 hours; chronic is ≥48 hours. Unknown duration uses chronic correction safeguards in the European guideline.

fields.label: After-treatment response?
fields.help: First identify whether initial treatment has not started, is active, or has a documented response. An incomplete entry never implies a response.

fields.label: Cumulative Na correction?
fields.help: Track the dated total sodium rise against 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L later, or a clinician-agreed lower ODS-risk ceiling.
fields.essential: 10 mmol/L first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L later are correction limits, not targets; higher ODS-risk contexts need a lower individualized ceiling.

fields.label: Tonicity / urine pattern?
fields.help: In hypotonic hyponatraemia, interpret paired urine osmolality first and urine sodium second. Diuretics and kidney disease can confound this sequence.

quickReference.summary: Symptoms and attribution set emergency urgency; sodium alone never proves safety.
recognition: The European biochemical bands are mild 130 to <135, moderate 125 to <130 and profound <125 mmol/L; they do not by themselves determine an emergency response.
Severe symptoms include vomiting, cardio-respiratory distress, deep somnolence, seizures and coma. Moderately severe symptoms include nausea without vomiting, confusion and headache.
Symptoms are non-specific. Confirm the clinical causal link and keep alternative causes active, especially with mild biochemical hyponatraemia.
If duration is not established, use chronic correction safeguards unless clinical/history evidence supports acute onset.
redFlags: Accepted severe or moderately severe symptoms, rapid neurologic deterioration, seizure, coma, cardio-respiratory distress, or unsafe assessment context.

A documented sodium rise >10 mmol/L in the first 24 h or >8 mmol/L in a later 24 h, or a higher-ODS-risk context such as sodium ≤105, alcohol use disorder, hypokalaemia, malnutrition or advanced liver disease.
Rapid urine output after restoring volume, falling sodium despite treatment, or persistent symptoms after a documented sodium response.

steps.text: Verify sodium, classify symptoms, and decide whether their causal relation to hyponatraemia is clinically accepted. Do not use a biochemical band alone as an emergency label.

In a close-monitoring environment, the Society 2022 emergency figure uses 150 mL 3% hypertonic saline over 20 minutes; check sodium after 20 minutes while the next bolus is begun, repeated up to two more times or until a 5 mmol/L rise.
steps.dosingNote: Guideline reminder only; confirm local product, protocol and authority.

steps.text: After a documented 5 mmol/L rise with symptom improvement, stop hypertonic saline, use minimum feasible 0.9% saline to keep the line open, and begin cause-specific treatment. If symptoms do not improve, urgently reassess other causes and use the active emergency protocol.

Exclude non-hypotonic causes. In hypotonic hyponatraemia, interpret paired urine osmolality first and urine sodium second; account for volume status, diuretics, renal disease and adrenal/pituitary/thyroid causes before assigning SIAD.

Treat 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L in each later 24 hours as limits, not targets. Higher ODS-risk contexts need a lower individualized ceiling. Calculate a dated running total and respond to documented overcorrection with expert-guided relowering rather than an auto-generated regimen.

monitoring: During the Society emergency bolus sequence, check serum sodium after 20 minutes and reassess symptoms; do not infer the response if no serial result is entered.
After a documented 5 mmol/L rise with symptom improvement, the Society figure says sodium at 6 hours, 12 hours and daily until stable under stable treatment.
The European guideline suggests sodium every 6 hours for moderate/profound chronic hyponatraemia until stable; if active 3% infusion continues, it suggests every 4 hours.
After volume restoration, sudden urine output >100 mL/hour can signal rapid auto-correction; the European guidance advises sodium every 2 hours until stable in that circumstance.

entry.title: Does this meet AKI criteria?
entry.guidance: Any one criterion establishes AKI. Missing baseline or timing stays unconfirmed.

fields.label: Creatinine rise in 48 hours
fields.threshold: At least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours
fields.definition: Serum creatinine rose by at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours.

fields.label: Creatinine relative to baseline
fields.threshold: At least 1.5 times baseline within 7 days
fields.definition: Serum creatinine reached at least 1.5 times a known or presumed baseline within the prior 7 days.

fields.label: Urine output observation
fields.threshold: Below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours
fields.definition: Urine volume was below 0.5 mL/kg/h for a defined 6-hour observation window.

entry.text: Any one criterion establishes AKI. Missing baseline or timing stays unconfirmed.

fields.label: Creatinine rise in 48 hours
fields.threshold: At least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours
fields.definition: Serum creatinine rose by at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours.
fields.help: Any one fully assessed criterion establishes AKI. Missing baseline, comparator timing, body weight, or a defined urine-output observation interval remains unconfirmed.

fields.label: Creatinine relative to baseline
fields.threshold: At least 1.5 times baseline within 7 days
fields.definition: Serum creatinine reached at least 1.5 times a known or presumed baseline within the prior 7 days.
fields.help: Any one fully assessed criterion establishes AKI. Missing baseline, comparator timing, body weight, or a defined urine-output observation interval remains unconfirmed.

fields.label: Urine output observation
fields.threshold: Below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours
fields.definition: Urine volume was below 0.5 mL/kg/h for a defined 6-hour observation window.
fields.help: Any one fully assessed criterion establishes AKI. Missing baseline, comparator timing, body weight, or a defined urine-output observation interval remains unconfirmed.

fields.label: Refractory life threat?
fields.help: For this field, a refractory life threat means hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, uraemic complications, fluid overload or pulmonary oedema that is not responding to medical management. It requires immediate escalation.
fields.essential: Refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, uraemic complications, fluid overload, or pulmonary oedema despite medical management.

fields.label: Volume / perfusion picture?
fields.help: Choose this from the current physiology, not from AKI alone. The depletion option excludes haemorrhagic shock, which needs its own emergency haemorrhage pathway. Congestion does not make diuretics a treatment for AKI itself.

fields.label: Obstruction or cause concern?
fields.help: Suspected pyonephrosis means possible infected upper-tract obstruction and needs immediate action. In AKI, an unknown cause or obstruction risk calls for urinary-tract ultrasound within 24 hours; suspected pyonephrosis needs ultrasound within 6 hours.

fields.label: Nephrology referral feature?
fields.help: NICE advises nephrology discussion within 24 hours for possible specialist kidney disease (such as vasculitis, glomerulonephritis, tubulointerstitial nephritis or myeloma), no clear cause, inadequate response, AKI complications, stage 3 AKI, transplant, or CKD stage 4–5. A clear cause that responds promptly usually does not need routine referral, except in transplant recipients.
fields.essential: Stage 3, unclear or nonresponsive AKI, complications, suspected specialist kidney disease, transplant, or CKD stage 4–5.

fields.label: Medicine / contrast risk?
fields.help: Review potentially kidney-harmful or renally cleared medicines, interactions, therapeutic-drug monitoring needs and recent contrast. A changing creatinine does not prove stable drug clearance.

stages.title: Recognize
stages.empty: Verify the AKI data before assigning a stage.

stages.title: Treat life threats
stages.empty: No medical-refractory RRT trigger entered.

stages.title: Assess perfusion
stages.empty: AKI alone does not select a fluid maneuver.

stages.title: Look for cause
stages.empty: Continue cause-directed assessment.

stages.title: Monitor & refer
stages.empty: Set follow-up to the clinical trajectory.

quickReference.summary: Confirm actual creatinine/urine timing, treat complications first, choose fluid strategy from physiology, then find the cause and set monitoring/referral.
recognition: KDIGO AKI: creatinine rise ≥0.3 mg/dL in 48 h, ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h.
Use the worse creatinine or urine-output stage; do not invent a baseline or a urine-output window.
A changing creatinine is not a stable eGFR/CrCl drug-clearance estimate.
redFlags: Hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, pulmonary oedema/fluid overload or uraemic complication not responding to medical management.
Suspected infected obstruction/pyonephrosis, anuria, shock, rapidly worsening trajectory or impaired oxygenation.
Stage 3, transplant, CKD stage 4–5, unclear/nonresponsive AKI, complication or suspected specialist kidney disease.

steps.text: Confirm time-stamped creatinine and observed urine output; stage by the worse criterion.
Escalate refractory potassium, acid-base, uraemic or pulmonary-oedema/fluid-overload complications without waiting for a creatinine threshold.
Use isotonic crystalloid only for credible depletion and reassess response; avoid reflex fluid loading in congestion. Vasomotor shock requires a local fluids-plus-vasopressor plan.
Urinalysis promptly; ultrasound within 6 h for suspected pyonephrosis and within 24 h for unknown cause/obstruction risk. Review medicines and contrast urgency.
Set creatinine, electrolyte and urine-output timing; discuss qualifying AKI with nephrology within 24 h, or immediately for RRT indications.

monitoring: Monitor serum creatinine and a defined urine-output interval; daily creatinine is typical in hospital but frequency follows clinical need.
Trend potassium, acid-base status, volume balance, weight/congestion and response to each intervention.
After AKI, monitor creatinine based on stability and degree of recovery; NICE considers nephrology referral after recovery when eGFR is 30 mL/min/1.73 m² or less.

The Society acute guidance (2016) and its 2019 addendum govern the emergency wording; the 2025 ESE guideline is used only for established chronic hypoparathyroidism and explicitly excludes studies primarily selecting end-stage renal disease.

The 2019 addendum makes calcium salts non-volume-equivalent. This module exposes only calcium-gluconate source actions and never treats local calcium chloride as a gluconate equivalent or selects a chloride product.

The IV route is source detail, not an order. This aid never selects an infusion pump, line, dilution, volume, repeat dose, calcium-chloride conversion, local concentration or automatic replacement schedule.

End-stage renal failure/dialysis blocks the general large-volume infusion and chronic oral/active-vitamin-D resource links. Severe symptoms remain urgent and require renal/monitored-care decisions outside this engine.
A product listing establishes only product identity, not availability, suitability, dose, route safety, prescribing authorization or an approved local regimen.

entry.title: Calcium below the local reference range; adjusted Ca <1.9 mmol/L is severe.
entry.scope: Ionised calcium can establish a low result; do not assign an unadjusted total value to an adjusted-calcium treatment band.

fields.label: Verified calcium status?
fields.help: The Society acute threshold uses albumin-adjusted calcium. Ionised calcium can confirm hypocalcaemia, but an unadjusted total-calcium value is not assigned a treatment band here.
fields.essential: Calcium below the local reference range; adjusted Ca <1.9 mmol/L is severe.

fields.label: Symptoms / ECG feature?
fields.help: Emergency features include seizure, laryngospasm, prolonged QT or arrhythmia. Other symptoms include tetany, carpopedal spasm and paraesthesia. “None” requires active assessment.
fields.essential: Emergency features: seizure, laryngospasm, prolonged QT or arrhythmia. “None” requires active assessment.

fields.label: IV calcium treatment phase?
fields.help: Choose a documented phase. “Resolved” means symptoms improved after IV calcium; it does not establish normocalcaemia or a completed cause-treatment plan.

fields.label: Oral route safe?
fields.help: Safe requires an appropriate swallow, GI absorption and an available formulation. An unsafe or unknown route is not converted into an automatic IV-calcium indication for otherwise mild asymptomatic hypocalcaemia.

fields.label: Renal / dialysis status?
fields.help: Dialysis includes end-stage kidney failure on dialysis. It blocks this guide’s large-volume infusion and chronic oral/active-vitamin-D resource links; it does not make severe symptoms benign.

fields.label: Magnesium status?
fields.help: Low magnesium can impair PTH secretion and action. Correcting a documented deficit is part of cause treatment, but must not delay urgent calcium rescue for a severe symptomatic presentation.

fields.label: Likely cause context?
fields.help: Use a reviewed context, not a diagnosis made by this aid. The source work-up includes phosphate, PTH, vitamin D, magnesium and kidney function alongside calcium and albumin/ionised calcium.

stages.empty: Select a route only from established severity and phase.

quickReference.summary: Verify calcium physiology, triage symptoms and ECG, distinguish monitored IV rescue from mild oral review, then correct the cause and measure the response.
recognition: Society guidance defines severe hypocalcaemia as adjusted calcium <1.9 mmol/L and/or symptoms at any low calcium value. Symptoms may be rate-dependent, so a number alone does not prove safety.
Urgent features include seizure, laryngospasm, tetany/carpopedal spasm, prolonged QT and arrhythmia. Assess airway, neurologic state and ECG while confirming calcium physiology.
Initial cause work-up includes adjusted or ionised calcium context, phosphate, PTH, kidney function, vitamin D and magnesium.
redFlags: Adjusted calcium <1.9 mmol/L, seizure, laryngospasm, tetany, prolonged QT, arrhythmia, or a rapidly deteriorating clinical state.
Current or recent IV calcium with missing calcium trend, treatment phase, elemental-calcium amount, ECG result, line details or response.

Dialysis/end-stage kidney failure, renal impairment, hypomagnesaemia, hyperphosphataemia, post-neck surgery, low/inappropriately normal PTH, vitamin-D deficiency, pancreatitis, rhabdomyolysis or large-volume transfusion.

steps.text: Use albumin-adjusted or ionised calcium and assess seizure, airway, tetany and QT/rhythm features. Do not let cause work-up delay emergency assessment.
Society guidance uses 10–20 mL 10% calcium gluconate in 50–100 mL 5% dextrose IV over 10 minutes with ECG monitoring, repeated only under reassessment until asymptomatic.
steps.dosingNote: Source reminder only: confirm the actual gluconate product, elemental calcium, dilution, line, pump, renal status and local authority.

steps.text: The Society mild branch uses oral calcium when adjusted calcium is above 1.9 mmol/L and symptoms are absent. For established chronic HypoPT, ESE advises adequate elemental calcium intake and splitting supplemental elemental calcium above 500 mg/day.
steps.dosingNote: Do not convert source elemental-calcium guidance into a local tablet count without product and renal review.

steps.text: Use secure-line, dilution and ECG safeguards for IV calcium. Do not mix calcium gluconate with bicarbonate- or phosphate-containing fluids. Dialysis blocks the generic large-volume infusion branch.
Check and correct magnesium, clarify PTH/vitamin-D/acute-process causes, and document serial calcium, symptoms, ECG and renal context. Symptom improvement does not prove normocalcaemia.

monitoring: During intermittent calcium-gluconate infusion, the May 2026 label measures serum calcium every 4–6 hours; during continuous infusion, every 1–4 hours. These are source points, not auto-scheduled observations.
Use ECG monitoring during emergency IV calcium; continuous ECG monitoring is specifically called for with arrhythmia or digoxin context in the Society guidance.

For established chronic HypoPT after a treatment change, the 2025 ESE guideline recommends biochemical reassessment every 1–2 weeks, then regular calcium/phosphate/magnesium/creatinine review when stable. Dialysis needs its own renal plan.

The Society for Endocrinology acute guidance remains listed on its live guidance page; the Endocrine Society HCM resource remains listed as last updated December 2022. This review did not identify a later replacement on those official pages as checked 15 September 2026.
The Endocrine Society denosumab/bisphosphonate recommendations apply to accepted hypercalcaemia of malignancy. The engine does not apply them to a general or non-HCM cause selection.

General non-HCM IV bisphosphonate access also needs an explicit rehydrated-persistent-calcium state. Unknown entries never establish absence of overload, renal impairment, prior treatment or treatment failure.

Calcitonin is only surfaced as a severe-HCM bridge with a documented non-exposure state and is limited to 48–72 hours because of tachyphylaxis. No dose, repeat course or product is auto-selected from a missing treatment record.
No HIS connection, patient data, order staging, order submission, product-equivalence decision or local formulary claim is contained in this data layer.

entry.title: Calcium above the local reference range; treatment bands use adjusted total calcium.
entry.scope: Do not place an ionised value in a total-calcium band. Cause and prior treatment determine the next action.

fields.label: Verified adjusted calcium?
fields.help: Use albumin-adjusted total calcium when available. The mild band is only for a result above the local reference range and below 3.0 mmol/L; do not convert ionized calcium into a total-calcium band here.
fields.essential: Calcium above the local reference range; treatment bands use adjusted total calcium.

fields.label: Urgent clinical features?
fields.help: Crisis features include coma, marked confusion, dysrhythmia, major conduction change or hemodynamic instability. Other symptoms include thirst/polyuria, nausea, constipation, weakness and cognitive change.

fields.label: Volume / fluid tolerance?
fields.help: The emergency saline range applies only to documented depletion when vigorous rehydration is tolerable. “Rehydrated; high Ca persists” needs a timed calcium response, current fluid tolerance and renal assessment. Heart failure or existing overload needs a response-guided plan.

fields.label: Renal reserve / dialysis?
fields.help: Assess current kidney function before IV bisphosphonate. Severe renal failure or dialysis changes both fluid and antiresorptive decisions.

fields.label: Cause / malignancy context?
fields.help: PTH-dependent and PTH-independent causes need different plans. Select malignancy only when the clinical team accepts it as the cause; do not infer HCM from cancer history alone.

fields.label: Antiresorptive / response?
fields.help: Reconcile the actual agent and timing. “Persistent after IV BP” is a clinician-documented HCM response state, not an inferred lack of response.

fields.label: Calcitonin exposure?
fields.help: Calcitonin is a short bridge, not a recurring default. The HCM guideline limits it to 48–72 hours because tachyphylaxis develops.

quickReference.summary: Classify urgency, fluid tolerance and cause before adding a calcium-lowering treatment.
recognition: Use the below-3.0 band only for calcium above the local reference range; a reviewed not-high result does not activate this acute treatment guide. The Society bands then place 3.0–3.5 mmol/L in prompt review and above 3.5 mmol/L in urgent correction review.
Coma, marked confusion, dysrhythmia, conduction change, hemodynamic instability, renal impairment and severe dehydration can override a reassuring-looking history or a single calcium result.
Check calcium measurement context, albumin, phosphate, PTH, renal function, ECG, fluid balance, medicines/supplements and the likely cause. Do not infer HCM from cancer history alone.
redFlags: Adjusted calcium above 3.5 mmol/L; coma, marked confusion, arrhythmia, major conduction change or hemodynamic instability.
Severe renal failure/dialysis, pulmonary congestion, heart failure or overload that makes the standard rehydration range unsafe.
Persistent/recurrent accepted HCM after IV bisphosphonate, calcitonin beyond 72 hours, or a calcitriol-mediated HCM pattern without a documented glucocorticoid response.

steps.text: Verify the calcium measure and albumin context, assess cognition, ECG/rhythm, renal function and fluid balance, and escalate a crisis presentation immediately.

The Society source uses 0.9% saline 4–6 L in 24 hours only for a depleted adult who can tolerate vigorous rehydration. For general non-HCM IV bisphosphonate review, document that rehydration was tolerated and calcium remains high on a timed recheck. Heart failure, overload or severe renal disease needs a response-guided plan rather than a fixed volume.
steps.dosingNote: Loop diuretics are not routine calcium-lowering therapy; use them only for overload that develops.

steps.text: The HCM antiresorptive guideline applies after malignancy is accepted as the cause. Non-HCM and unclassified causes need their own mechanism and renal review; do not carry a denosumab recommendation across those branches.

For general non-HCM IV bisphosphonate review, require the explicit post-rehydration persistent-calcium state and renal safeguards. Accepted HCM follows its distinct concurrent antiresorptive review; for refractory HCM after IV bisphosphonate, review denosumab. In calcitriol-mediated HCM, glucocorticoids come first.

steps.role: Use calcitonin only as a bridge
steps.text: For initial severe non-calcitriol HCM with documented no antiresorptive, calcitonin is an adjunct with one antiresorptive, limited to 48–72 hours. Reconcile exposure and response instead of repeating it by default.

monitoring: During active correction, trend calcium, fluid balance, renal function, symptoms and ECG concerns. No generic monitoring interval is safe for every acute presentation.
The Society guidance expects IV bisphosphonate calcium nadir at 2–4 days; a recent treatment entry does not establish failure or justify a duplicate dose.
For HCM, monitor magnesium and phosphate and replace as clinically appropriate; review dental health and vitamin-D status before antiresorptive treatment where time and clinical condition permit.

entry.title: Measured Mg <0.7 mmol/L; <0.5 is the severe biochemical band.
entry.scope: Cardiac or neurologic danger requires assessment even before the result is confirmed.

fields.label: Magnesium result?
fields.help: SPS defines hypomagnesaemia as serum magnesium below 0.7 mmol/L. Its mild band is 0.5 to 0.7 mmol/L and severe is below 0.5 mmol/L. Use an actual time-linked result; unknown is not normal.
fields.essential: Measured Mg <0.7 mmol/L; <0.5 is the severe biochemical band.

fields.label: Severe neuro / cardiac feature?
fields.help: SPS lists nystagmus, tetany, seizures and cardiac arrhythmias as severe features. A feature can need emergency assessment even if the magnesium result has not yet been verified or does not explain it.
fields.essential: Severe features: nystagmus, tetany, seizure or arrhythmia.

fields.label: Enteral route usable?
fields.help: Usable means safe swallowing, a functioning gastrointestinal route and an appropriate formulation. Severe deficit, limited absorption, nil by mouth status or a need for immediate correction can make oral treatment unsuitable.

fields.label: Kidney risk context?
fields.help: SPS advises specialist input before replacement in AKI, CKD stage 4–5, dialysis or transplant. For CKD stage 1–3, use IV magnesium with caution and consider reducing its initial dose by 25–50%; SPS says oral magnesium needs no adjustment. This guide does not calculate an individual renal dose.

fields.label: Likely loss / contributor?
fields.help: SPS lists low intake, intestinal loss, medicine effects, renal loss and transcellular shift. Medicine contributors include aminoglycosides, loop or thiazide diuretics, proton-pump inhibitors and tacrolimus. This selector does not diagnose renal wasting.

fields.label: Low potassium or calcium?
fields.help: Hypomagnesaemia often coexists with hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia. Check and treat documented associated deficits with their own assessment and local protocol; this guide does not select their regimen.

quickReference.summary: Confirm the low magnesium result and emergency features, select a route only after renal review, address the cause, then measure response.
recognition: SPS defines hypomagnesaemia as serum magnesium below 0.7 mmol/L; <0.5 mmol/L is its severe band.
Severe features include nystagmus, tetany, seizures and cardiac arrhythmias.
Check potassium, calcium and renal function with a documented deficit; unknown findings are not normal findings.
redFlags: Seizure, tetany, nystagmus, arrhythmia, haemodynamic concern or other active emergency physiology.
Magnesium <0.5 mmol/L, inability to use the enteral route, persistent GI loss or recurrent unexplained deficit.
AKI, CKD stage 4–5, dialysis, transplant, uncertain renal clearance or an uncertain emergency feature. In CKD stage 1–3, IV magnesium needs a cautious local dose review.

steps.text: Record the actual serum magnesium, symptoms, potassium, calcium and renal context. Do not infer a normal value or a mild band.
Severe neurologic or cardiac features need monitored emergency assessment; do not wait for routine replacement planning.
SPS uses oral replacement for eligible mild deficiency and hospital IV magnesium for severe/symptomatic deficiency or an unavailable enteral route. Verify local product, dilution and monitoring.
Address GI loss/absorption, medicines, renal-loss context and documented potassium or calcium deficits.
After IV magnesium, measure magnesium after each dose; with oral therapy, SPS suggests review at 7 days and again at 1–3 months according to cause.

monitoring: During replacement, monitor magnesium, potassium, calcium, renal function and blood pressure; use ECG monitoring for severe symptoms.
Oral magnesium may be poorly absorbed and cause diarrhoea. Do not turn local antacid/laxative products into an unverified replacement conversion.
In advanced kidney disease, AKI, dialysis or transplant, obtain a specialist plan rather than applying a generic renal dose.

entry.title: Measured Mg >1.05 mmol/L; >2.5 is the source severe band.
entry.scope: Assess breathing, reflexes, ECG and renal clearance; coordinate intentional obstetric magnesium with the obstetric team.

fields.label: Magnesium result?
fields.help: Queensland Health calls severe hypermagnesaemia above 2.5 mmol/L. The magnesium-sulfate SmPC notes that manifestations overlap across concentrations; a result alone does not replace assessment of reflexes, breathing, consciousness, blood pressure or ECG.
fields.essential: Measured Mg >1.05 mmol/L; >2.5 is the source severe band.

fields.label: Neuro / respiratory toxicity?
fields.help: Concerning findings include loss of deep-tendon reflexes, weakness or paralysis, respiratory depression, reduced consciousness and hypotension. These require emergency assessment; they are not automatically explained by a magnesium value.
fields.essential: Toxicity: lost reflexes, weakness/paralysis, respiratory depression, reduced consciousness or hypotension.

fields.label: ECG / conduction concern?
fields.help: The SmPC describes bradycardia, conduction/ECG change, arrhythmia and cardiac arrest with magnesium toxicity. A reviewed ECG finding changes urgency; an unknown ECG does not mean a normal ECG.

fields.label: Mg exposure / obstetric therapy?
fields.help: Queensland Health advises reviewing magnesium-containing antacids, enemas, supplements and medicines. Magnesium can be deliberately used in pregnancy for eclampsia/pre-eclampsia; contact the obstetric team before altering prescribed maternal therapy.

fields.label: Renal dysfunction / dialysis?
fields.help: Severe renal dysfunction limits magnesium elimination. The SmPC says peritoneal dialysis or haemodialysis rapidly lowers magnesium in this setting; it does not make dialysis an automatic action for every elevated result.

fields.label: Volume / urine clearance state?
fields.help: Queensland Health uses sodium chloride to promote kidney excretion only in an appropriate fluid/urine context, aiming for at least 60 mL/hour. Select “After saline” only when a clinician has assessed volume tolerance and a saline strategy has not achieved that urine target. Fluid overload, hypovolaemia, oliguria and severe renal dysfunction need a separate plan.

quickReference.summary: Confirm the high magnesium and toxicity, stabilize respiratory/cardiac risk, stop the source safely, then select clearance only after renal and volume review.
recognition: Queensland Health defines severe hypermagnesaemia as >2.5 mmol/L; clinical toxicity and trend remain decisive.
Check reflexes, weakness/paralysis, respiratory state, consciousness, blood pressure, ECG/conduction, calcium, potassium and renal function.
Review magnesium-containing prescribed, OTC and administered products, including antacids, enemas and supplements.
redFlags: Loss of deep-tendon reflexes, respiratory depression, paralysis, reduced consciousness, hypotension, bradycardia, conduction abnormality or arrhythmia.
Magnesium >2.5 mmol/L, rapidly rising level, oliguria/anuria, severe renal dysfunction or dialysis context.
Potential obstetric magnesium toxicity: obtain urgent support and coordinate with obstetrics before changing prescribed therapy.

steps.text: Verify magnesium and trend, then assess reflexes, breathing, consciousness, ECG and renal context. Unknown is not reassuring.

For confirmed high magnesium with toxicity, Queensland gives calcium gluconate 2.2 mmol in 0.9% sodium chloride over 5 minutes; repeat if needed. Its effect is immediate but transient and does not remove magnesium.
Review and hold a non-obstetric magnesium source through the responsible team. In pregnancy/eclampsia context, contact obstetrics before altering prescribed therapy.

For severe or symptomatic HyperMg, use renal excretion measures only when volume tolerance and urine output are established. Consider a loop only after the source saline/urine strategy; limited clearance may need renal/critical-care discussion.
Trend magnesium, calcium, potassium, renal function, reflexes, respiration and ECG/rhythm. Initial calcium response is not magnesium clearance.

monitoring: Set serial magnesium and clinical observation timing to toxicity, kidney function and clearance strategy; do not apply one generic interval to every case.
Document exposure cessation, urine output, fluid balance, ECG/rhythm, reflexes, respiratory state and changes in consciousness.
For severe renal dysfunction, the SmPC says peritoneal dialysis or haemodialysis can rapidly lower magnesium, but the decision remains clinician-owned.

guides.title: Hypernatremia
guides.reviewNotice: The frozen review keeps the adult clinical review, hospital page, and established-CDI guidance in their distinct scopes. Its correction limits are safeguards, not universal adult targets or local policy.
guides.guideVersion: Adult hypernatraemia clinical review (2023), NHS Ayrshire & Arran hospital guidance (reviewed January 2026; updated May 2026), and Society for Endocrinology established-CDI guidance (2018), as recorded in the frozen source review.
guides.resourceNotice: Internal hospital resource tables are omitted from this shared edition.
guides.scope: Adult hypernatraemia: triage, perfusion, correction safeguards, and cause review.
reviewLimitations: This is compact adult decision support, not a local protocol, prescription, fluid calculator, infusion plan, order set, or patient-specific treatment plan.

The core adult source is a 2023 clinical review, not a national adult hypernatraemia guideline. A 2025 scoping review found only two randomized trials among 200 studies and concluded that current evidence cannot establish the safety or efficacy of specific therapies. The prototype therefore presents conservative safeguards and clinician-owned reassessment rather than a universal dose or rate.

The current NHS Ayrshire & Arran page supports a general 10 mmol/L/day caution; Society for Endocrinology guidance is authoritative but limited to established cranial DI. Neither is represented as a universal local policy. The source differences are disclosed rather than silently harmonized.

The engine never calculates free-water deficit, body-water fraction, maintenance need, ongoing loss, fluid rate, bag count, DDAVP dose, dialysis prescription or target sodium. It never treats a missing result as normal, a missing correction total as within ceiling, or a suspected DI pattern as central DI.

Acute symptomatic sodium-loading hypernatraemia, severe/changing renal dysfunction, dialysis, fluid overload, shock, pregnancy, pediatric care, HHS/DKA, toxic ingestion and complex DI require condition-specific senior/endocrine/nephrology/critical-care management.
A product listing establishes only product identity. It does not establish current availability, orderability, patient suitability, dose, route, monitoring requirements or authorization to prescribe.

entry.title: Measured Na above 145 mmol/L
entry.scope: Assess perfusion before water replacement. Unknown sodium, neurologic status, fluid risk, duration, route, cause, or correction state does not establish a safe treatment branch.

fields.label: Sodium band · mmol/L
fields.help: Use a current credible serum sodium result. The adult clinical review defines hypernatraemia as above 145 mmol/L and lists 146–150, 151–155 and above 155 mmol/L bands. This guide combines the middle bands; a result at or below 145 mmol/L does not activate a hypernatraemia fluid branch.
fields.essential: Hypernatraemia is measured serum sodium above 145 mmol/L. The reviewed bands are >145 to 155 and >155 mmol/L; a value at or below 145 does not enter a hypernatraemia water-replacement branch.

fields.label: Urgent neurologic feature?
fields.help: Present means seizure, coma, marked confusion, reduced consciousness, focal deficit, or a clearly acute neurologic deterioration. It triggers emergency assessment but does not prove that sodium is its cause. Absent requires an active assessment.

fields.label: Perfusion / fluid-risk state?
fields.help: Choose shock only for documented hypotension or poor perfusion. “Depleted, perfused” requires review of congestion and renal fluid tolerance. “No depletion” also requires that no major fluid-risk concern was reviewed. The high-risk option includes fluid overload, decompensated heart failure, advanced or changing renal dysfunction, oliguria, or dialysis.

fields.label: Duration of high sodium?
fields.help: Acute means a documented onset within 48 hours. Chronic means more than 48 hours. Unknown is handled with the chronic/unknown correction safeguard; it is not evidence of acute onset.

fields.label: Water route available?
fields.help: Oral/NG usable means the patient can safely receive and retain enteral water. IV needed means enteral water is not currently usable but IV access and fluid tolerance have been reviewed. Unknown does not select a route.

fields.label: Cause / urine pattern?
fields.help: Use only a reviewed pattern. Dilute polyuria can raise concern for DI but does not establish central DI or a desmopressin indication. Known CDI means an established diagnosis and existing specialist plan. Hypertonic sodium gain is distinct from water-loss hypernatraemia.

fields.label: Correction state?
fields.help: Not started means no sodium-lowering water or DDAVP treatment is currently being given for this episode. Active requires a reviewed route, rate, timed sodium total and response. The fast-fall option is clinician-entered when sodium is falling faster than the agreed rate or 24-hour ceiling; missing serial values never establish that finding.

quickReference.summary: Confirm sodium and urgency, restore perfusion first, then use a measured water and cause plan.
recognition: Hypernatraemia is serum sodium above 145 mmol/L. Review the current value, timing, trend, glucose, tonicity, neurologic state, water access, intake/output, volume and fluid-risk context before choosing treatment.

For chronic or unknown duration, this prototype uses a conservative guard of no faster than 0.5 mmol/L/hour and no more than 10 mmol/L/24 hours. These are limits for a clinician-owned plan, not a declaration of safety or a correction target.

Urgent neurologic deterioration, shock/hypotension, sodium above 155 mmol/L, sodium gain, severe/changing renal dysfunction, dialysis, overload and high-volume dilute urine require more than a simple water-deficit estimate.
redFlags: Seizure, coma, marked confusion, reduced consciousness or focal neurologic deterioration.
Shock/hypotension, sodium above 155 mmol/L, rapidly changing sodium, documented fast sodium fall or a breached correction ceiling.
Known CDI with missed/uncertain DDAVP, high-volume dilute urine, poor water access, fluid overload, decompensated heart failure, changing renal function or dialysis.

steps.text: Confirm a credible sodium result, glucose/tonicity context, trend and neurologic status. Urgent neurologic features need emergency assessment and should not be attributed to sodium by default.
For shock or hypotension, use a monitored 0.9% saline or balanced-crystalloid resuscitation pathway until volume is restored, then re-enter the fluid state before choosing free water.

For chronic or unknown duration, keep the rate at or below 0.5 mmol/L/hour and the 24-hour fall at or below 10 mmol/L. A documented fast fall or breached ceiling requires urgent reconciliation, not another default fluid action.

After perfusion and fluid risk are reviewed, use a clinician-set oral/NG, D5W or 0.45% saline plan based on route, volume state, losses and serial sodium. Do not convert a package volume or deficit formula into an automatic rate.

Dilute polyuria requires a DI differential. Only established CDI with a reviewed plan can surface DDAVP resource review; repeat sodium, urine output, fluid balance and glucose when relevant before changing therapy.

monitoring: Time-stamp baseline and repeat sodium values, every fluid and DDAVP exposure, urine output, fluid balance, neurologic status, perfusion and glucose with D5W. Missing serial values do not establish a safe correction trajectory.

The current NHS page asks for reassessment and recording at least every 8 hours in its severe-case pathway. Society for Endocrinology CDI guidance uses sodium every 4 hours during fluid resuscitation and no less often than every 12 hours until stable. Select a more frequent local plan when acuity or loss requires it.

Review renal trajectory, congestion, dialysis status and measured ongoing losses before changing water, saline or DDAVP exposure. Do not auto-repeat a prior product or declare the episode resolved from one result.

entry.title: Does this meet DKA or HHS criteria?
entry.guidance: Use time-linked presentation findings before treatment changed the results. Missing findings do not exclude DKA/HHS.

fields.label: Presentation glucose?
fields.help: DKA accepts glucose at least 200 mg/dL (about 11.1 mmol/L) or a prior history of diabetes. HHS requires glucose at least 600 mg/dL (about 33.3 mmol/L). These are presentation findings, not a treatment-phase glucose target.

fields.label: Prior diabetes history?
fields.help: A prior diabetes history can satisfy the first DKA diagnostic component at any presentation glucose. No known history does not turn a glucose below 200 mg/dL with ketoacidosis into reassurance; review the clinical differential.

fields.label: Presentation ketones?
fields.help: Prefer quantitative beta-hydroxybutyrate (BOHB): below 3.0 vs at least 3.0 mmol/L. If BOHB is unavailable, urine ketones below 2+ vs at least 2+ are the Figure 2 alternative. Urine nitroprusside reflects acetoacetate, can understate early ketonaemia and overstate it during recovery; record the method and use clinician review.

fields.label: Presentation pH?
fields.help: DKA acidosis uses pH below 7.30; the HHS absence-of-acidosis component requires pH at least 7.30 and bicarbonate at least 15 mmol/L.

fields.label: Presentation bicarbonate?
fields.help: DKA acidosis uses bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L. HHS diagnosis accepts bicarbonate at least 15 mmol/L, but the isolated-HHS insulin branch requires bicarbonate at least 18 mmol/L; 15 to below 18 can therefore meet HHS diagnosis while routing to the mixed treatment pattern.

fields.label: Presentation osmolality?
fields.help: HHS hyperosmolality is calculated effective serum osmolality above 300 mOsm/kg or total serum osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg. The consensus uses strict greater-than thresholds. This module accepts only a reviewed categorical finding; it does not calculate osmolality.

entry.text: Use presentation findings before treatment changed the results. The treatment pattern is derived; missing findings do not exclude DKA/HHS.
entry.scope: Show all three DKA and all four HHS criteria before current-treatment findings. Shock or altered consciousness remains an independent escalation screen.

fields.label: Critical feature present?
fields.help: Select yes for shock, major haemodynamic compromise, altered consciousness, severe DKA, or a critical precipitating illness. Confirmed HHS has its own ICU-level destination action even when no additional critical feature is recorded.
fields.essential: Critical feature: shock, major haemodynamic compromise, altered consciousness, severe DKA, or a critical precipitating illness. Assess and escalate independently while diagnostic findings are completed.

fields.label: Presentation glucose?
fields.help: DKA accepts glucose at least 200 mg/dL (about 11.1 mmol/L) or a prior history of diabetes. HHS requires glucose at least 600 mg/dL (about 33.3 mmol/L). These are presentation findings, not a treatment-phase glucose target.

fields.label: Prior diabetes history?
fields.help: A prior diabetes history can satisfy the first DKA diagnostic component at any presentation glucose. No known history does not turn a glucose below 200 mg/dL with ketoacidosis into reassurance; review the clinical differential.

fields.label: Presentation ketones?
fields.help: Prefer quantitative beta-hydroxybutyrate (BOHB): below 3.0 vs at least 3.0 mmol/L. If BOHB is unavailable, urine ketones below 2+ vs at least 2+ are the Figure 2 alternative. Urine nitroprusside reflects acetoacetate, can understate early ketonaemia and overstate it during recovery; record the method and use clinician review.

fields.label: Presentation pH?
fields.help: DKA acidosis uses pH below 7.30; the HHS absence-of-acidosis component requires pH at least 7.30 and bicarbonate at least 15 mmol/L.

fields.label: Presentation bicarbonate?
fields.help: DKA acidosis uses bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L. HHS diagnosis accepts bicarbonate at least 15 mmol/L, but the isolated-HHS insulin branch requires bicarbonate at least 18 mmol/L; 15 to below 18 can therefore meet HHS diagnosis while routing to the mixed treatment pattern.

fields.label: Presentation osmolality?
fields.help: HHS hyperosmolality is calculated effective serum osmolality above 300 mOsm/kg or total serum osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg. The consensus uses strict greater-than thresholds. This module accepts only a reviewed categorical finding; it does not calculate osmolality.

fields.label: Perfusion / volume state?
fields.help: A depletion choice records bedside assessment, not a generic fluid indication. Renal/urine context is entered separately. High risk includes fluid overload, heart failure or a setting where a standard initial rate is unsafe. After intravascular restoration, choose subsequent fluid from blood pressure, heart rate, input/output and sodium rather than carrying forward an initial rate.

fields.label: Kidney function / urine output?
options: Oliguria, dialysis or major renal risk
fields.help: Adequate means observed urine output above 0.5 mL/kg/hour over a reviewed interval, with no major renal-risk context. Exactly 0.5 does not meet the HHS resolution endpoint; keep the endpoint unresolved for review. Oliguria, dialysis or advanced kidney disease needs a cautious fluid and potassium plan. This field does not estimate drug clearance.

fields.label: Potassium (mmol/L)?
fields.help: For potassium below 3.5 mmol/L, the consensus says start replacement at 10 mmol/hour and delay insulin until potassium is above 3.5. Exactly 3.5 does not prove a previously low result has risen above 3.5; confirm the trend before restarting insulin. Routine replacement starts only after potassium falls below 5.0, with a usual target of 4–5 mmol/L.

fields.label: Glucose / dextrose phase?
fields.help: These are glucose bands, not diagnostic labels. Euglycaemic DKA is derived only when verified DKA presents initially below 200 mg/dL with ketosis and acidosis. During active DKA or mixed crisis, glucose below 250 mg/dL triggers dextrose support so insulin can continue for ketosis. HHS may pass through the lower bands during active treatment; this guide exposes its dextrose review only with an in-limit trajectory, safe potassium, adequate renal/urine context and ongoing insulin need. Glucose alone never establishes resolution. A true hypoglycaemic value needs its own immediate rescue assessment.

fields.label: HHS correction trajectory?
fields.help: For HHS, keep glucose decline no faster than 90–120 mg/dL/hour, sodium decline no faster than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours, and osmolality fall within 3–8 mOsm/kg/hour. A sodium rise during early glucose correction alone is not an indication for hypotonic fluid. Enter a neurologic change under critical features; it does not itself prove a measured correction limit was exceeded. This finding applies to HHS or mixed presentations only.

fields.label: Care phase?
fields.help: DKA resolution requires beta-hydroxybutyrate below 0.6 mmol/L and venous pH at least 7.3 or bicarbonate at least 18 mmol/L; glucose below 200 mg/dL is ideal. HHS resolution requires osmolality below 300 mOsm/kg, glucose below 250 mg/dL, urine output above 0.5 mL/kg/hour and improved cognition. For mixed crisis, document both relevant endpoints before transition.

stages.empty: Verify the crisis pattern and treatment phase.

stages.title: Stabilize volume & urgency
stages.empty: Assess critical features, perfusion and fluid tolerance.

stages.title: Protect potassium & treat
stages.empty: Use verified potassium and glucose findings before a regimen branch.

stages.empty: Use the endpoint that matches the documented crisis pattern.

quickReference.summary: Verify the crisis pattern, protect potassium, use the correct DKA/HHS branch, then resolve the matching endpoint.
recognition: DKA needs diabetes or glucose at least 200 mg/dL, ketonaemia and metabolic acidosis. Euglycaemic DKA can occur below 200 mg/dL.

HHS recognition needs glucose at least 600 mg/dL, hyperosmolality, no significant ketonaemia and bicarbonate at least 15. The 0.05 isolated-HHS branch additionally requires bicarbonate at least 18; otherwise review the mixed branch.
Use quantitative beta-hydroxybutyrate when available. A test named “blood ketone” does not prove the assay reports the source units.
redFlags: Confirmed HHS, severe DKA, shock, altered consciousness or a critical precipitant: ICU-level care.
Potassium below 3.5 mmol/L: replace first and do not start or restart insulin until above 3.5 mmol/L.
HHS correction too fast, neurologic deterioration, oliguria/dialysis or fluid overload risk needs an immediate response-guided review.

steps.text: Record glucose, beta-hydroxybutyrate, venous pH/bicarbonate, electrolytes/renal function and osmolality before declaring DKA, HHS or mixed crisis.

Without cardiac/renal compromise: isotonic saline or balanced crystalloid 500–1,000 mL/hour for the first 2–4 hours. Cardiac/renal-risk contexts need small response-guided boluses and frequent reassessment.
Below 3.5 mmol/L: potassium 10 mmol/hour and hold insulin until above 3.5. Below 5.0 with adequate urine output: usual source maintenance is 20–30 mmol/L of IV fluid to target 4–5.

DKA or mixed: IV fixed-rate insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour. Isolated HHS: 0.05 units/kg/hour. At DKA glucose below 250, reduce insulin to 0.05 and add 5–10% dextrose; in active isolated HHS, review dextrose only when its trajectory, potassium, renal context and ongoing insulin need are documented.

Glucose every 1–2 hours; biochemical checks every 4 hours, with HHS osmolality every 4 hours. Use DKA ketone/pH/bicarbonate or HHS osmolality/glucose/urine/cognition endpoints, then give basal SC insulin at least 2 hours before ending IV insulin.

monitoring: During treatment: hospital-calibrated capillary glucose every 1–2 hours; electrolytes, creatinine, beta-hydroxybutyrate and venous pH every 4 hours until DKA resolves. In HHS, measure serum osmolality every 4 hours.
For HHS, keep glucose decline no faster than 90–120 mg/dL/hour, sodium decline no faster than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours, and osmolality fall within 3–8 mOsm/kg/hour.
Check potassium 2 hours after insulin starts and every 4 hours thereafter until DKA resolution; use closer local monitoring when a critical or renal-risk context requires it.

guides.title: Acute Hypotension
guides.reviewLabel: Upgraded · shock entry and reassessment review
guides.guideVersion: ESICM circulatory shock and haemodynamic monitoring guideline (2025), NICE CG174/NG253, SSC 2026, ESC ACS 2023, and RCUK special-circumstances guidance (2025), as recorded in the prototype review
guides.resourceNotice: Internal hospital resource tables are omitted from this shared edition.
guides.scope: Adult acute hypotension and suspected circulatory shock: entry, escalation, mechanism routing and response reassessment.
reviewLimitations: This is not a shock diagnosis, a blood-pressure calculator, a complete trauma/haemorrhage/cardiogenic-shock protocol, a fluid or vasopressor order, or a substitute for critical-care, procedural or specialty escalation.
Shock may occur without hypotension. Conversely, low BP alone does not establish hypoperfusion, fluid responsiveness or a safe fluid/pressor treatment path.

NICE NG253 (2025) uses reassessed 250 mL sepsis boluses, while SSC 2026 suggests at least 30 mL/kg in 3 hours for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock. The engine deliberately delegates this choice to the dedicated sepsis pathway and never combines the standards.

The NICE CG174 500 mL crystalloid criterion is limited here to credible non-haemorrhagic hypovolaemia with current hypoperfusion and no high/unknown fluid-harm concern; it never authorizes automatic repeats.

Norepinephrine is referenced only as a septic-shock critical-care handoff. Concentration, access, duration, monitoring, titration, add-on agents and patient-specific MAP target require the local protocol and clinician assessment.
Product availability, major-haemorrhage process, pressor safety, antimicrobial selection, anaphylaxis dosing and ACS treatment remain separately reviewed local work.

entry.title: Assess low BP and tissue perfusion separately.
entry.scope: Shock can occur without hypotension. Emergency assessment and cause-directed care proceed in parallel.

fields.label: Current circulation finding?
fields.help: Low BP: MAP <65 mmHg, SBP <90 mmHg or a major fall from baseline. Perfusion: mentation, capillary refill/skin, urine output and lactate in context. Shock is acute circulatory failure with hypoperfusion and can occur without low BP. Record the current assessed state, not a presumed diagnosis.
fields.essential: Low BP: MAP <65 mmHg, SBP <90 mmHg or a major baseline fall. Perfusion: mentation, capillary refill/skin, urine output and lactate in context.

fields.label: Immediate emergency priority?
fields.help: This priority is independent of the BP/perfusion answer. An emergency feature requires immediate ABCDE support and escalation even when the circulation entry is incomplete or appears improved.
fields.essential: Emergency: ABC compromise, altered consciousness, rapid deterioration or peri-arrest.

fields.label: Likely primary mechanism?
fields.help: Use haemorrhagic for active significant bleeding; hypovolaemic means non-haemorrhagic fluid loss. These choices name the physiology being acted on. Mixed or unclear shock stays unclassified and needs bedside echo/POCUS, ECG and cause review before a mechanism-specific fluid or pressor action.

fields.label: Fluid harm / overload concern?
fields.help: This is not a fluid-responsiveness test. Look for current congestion and fluid-harm risk; use dynamic response assessment and serial lung/perfusion review before any additional fluid.

fields.label: Current resuscitation phase?
fields.help: This is an assessment state, not a medication record. “Reassessment” and “refractory” do not authorize another bolus or a pressor dose; establish what was given, the response, and the cause.

fields.label: Time-critical cause cue?
fields.help: A cause cue routes urgent work in parallel. It does not prove the mechanism or import a routine fluid, pressor, antimicrobial, antithrombotic or anaphylaxis regimen into this guide.

stages.title: Reassess perfusion and route the cause

quickReference.summary: Separate low BP from hypoperfusion, escalate emergency features independently, classify physiology, and reassess response before any further fluid or pressor change.
recognition: Shock is acute circulatory failure with hypoperfusion; hypotension is common but is not required.
Low BP alone needs a credible repeat, baseline and tissue-perfusion assessment before it triggers a shock regimen.
Track mentation, capillary refill/skin perfusion, urine output, lactate/acid-base context and trajectory alongside BP/MAP.
redFlags: Airway/breathing compromise, altered consciousness, rapidly worsening trajectory or peri-arrest features.
Low BP plus hypoperfusion, or hypoperfusion despite apparently preserved BP.
Active major bleeding, suspected tamponade/tension pneumothorax/high-risk PE, cardiogenic congestion, or refractory hypoperfusion after initial response-guided treatment.

steps.text: Enter the current BP/perfusion state visibly. Unknown is not normal, and hypoperfusion can establish acute circulatory failure without hypotension.
Treat emergency ABCDE features independently of the circulation finding; call for urgent senior/critical-care help when perfusion persists or deteriorates.
Differentiate hypovolaemic, distributive, cardiogenic, obstructive and haemorrhagic physiology with bedside echo/POCUS, ECG, examination and targeted work-up.
For credible non-haemorrhagic hypovolaemia with low fluid-harm risk, NICE CG174 uses one 500 mL crystalloid bolus over less than 15 minutes. Reassess before any further fluid.
steps.dosingNote: Sepsis fluid standards are delegated to the dedicated sepsis pathway; do not combine them.

steps.text: Send suspected sepsis, ACS, anaphylaxis, bleeding or obstruction to its emergency pathway. Persistent shock needs critical-care review rather than an improvised pressor regimen.

monitoring: After every material intervention, trend BP/MAP, mentation, capillary refill/skin, urine output, lungs/oxygenation and lactate/acid-base context.
Use dynamic fluid-responsiveness assessment and serial echo where available; do not infer response from a single BP value.
For refractory shock or vasopressor use, escalate haemodynamic monitoring and cause control with critical care.

guides.title: Sepsis / Septic Shock
guides.guideVersion: SSC 2026 final + Sepsis-3 2016
guides.resourceNotice: Internal hospital resource tables are omitted from this shared edition.
guides.scope: Adult inpatient sepsis and septic-shock assessment, time-critical escalation, source review and reassessment.
reviewLimitations: SSC 2026 is the current final adult guideline located and read for this module. It was published on 23 March 2026 and updates the 2021 SSC guideline; no announced or draft update is used for its clinical branches.

The finding fields record clinical review; they do not diagnose infection or septic shock, calculate SOFA/qSOFA or fluid need, or replace emergency assessment. Age, microbiology and the septic-shock course must be explicitly reviewed; missing information stays unknown.

This module includes guideline-level spectrum, prolonged-infusion, de-escalation, steroid and fluid-removal review. It does not select an antimicrobial product or dose, infusion schedule, renal adjustment, local susceptibility assumption, fluid volume calculation, vasopressor preparation, corticosteroid regimen or source-control procedure.

Scope is adult inpatient recognition, early treatment and subsequent antimicrobial/hemodynamic review. It is not a complete implementation of all 129 SSC statements: detailed respiratory/ARDS support, prehospital systems, pediatric care and long-term rehabilitation require their dedicated pathways and the full guideline.

The SSC 30 mL/kg statement is shown only for life-threatening shock/hypoperfusion with a possible or probable/definite infectious context, an explicitly not-started phase, and reviewed absence of major overload/renal-cardiac risk. It is not repeated once resuscitation is in progress or post-initial, and it is not a local order or exemption from clinical reassessment.

Product orderability, pharmacy preparation, access safety, stewardship policy, procedural availability and clinician approval remain outside this data-only engine. Source alignment and current local availability are separate statuses.
