entry.title: Is acute organ dysfunction plausibly linked to infection?
entry.scope: Assess infection likelihood, organ dysfunction and shock separately. Sepsis is a clinical diagnosis; qSOFA is not a diagnostic gate.

fields.label: Adult age group?
fields.help: SSC 2026 suggests an initial MAP of 60–65 mm Hg in septic shock at age 65 or older. The general initial target is 65 mm Hg. Confirm an individual target against perfusion and comorbidity; this is not the diagnostic blood-pressure threshold.

fields.label: Infectious cause likelihood?
fields.help: This is a current clinical judgement about an infectious cause, not a culture result. It must remain distinct from organ dysfunction and shock. SSC 2026 asks for rapid assessment of infectious and noninfectious causes when sepsis is possible.

fields.label: Infection-linked organ dysfunction?
fields.help: Sepsis-3 describes sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection. In practice, confirm the acute change, plausible infection link, baseline and alternative causes; this form does not calculate SOFA or establish the diagnosis.
fields.essential: Review acute respiratory, mental-status, renal, liver or platelet changes against baseline and alternative causes.

fields.label: Shock / hypoperfusion now?
fields.help: Use the life-threatening choice for a clinician-recognized emergency physiology. It is deliberately separate from infection likelihood: shock remains urgent while infectious and noninfectious causes are reconciled. The form does not diagnose septic shock from one observation or calculate a score.
fields.essential: Shock/hypoperfusion is an urgent clinical assessment; a normal BP or one biomarker cannot exclude it.

fields.label: Resuscitation phase?
fields.help: Choose the current treatment phase, not the initial presentation. In progress or post-initial means that current fluids, vasopressors, timing and response must be reconciled before another initial-bolus recommendation is shown.

fields.label: Cultures / lactate status?
fields.help: This records whether relevant blood cultures and an initial lactate have actually been obtained or reviewed. Unknown is not a negative culture, normal lactate, or permission to delay time-critical treatment.

fields.label: Antimicrobial status?
fields.help: Record whether a first antimicrobial dose has actually been given for this episode and whether its time and regimen were reviewed. Unknown is not a not-started state. A dose already given routes to timing, regimen and ongoing-indication review rather than a duplicate first-dose instruction.

fields.label: Fluid overload / renal-cardiac risk
fields.help: Review pulmonary congestion, cardiac reserve, kidney trajectory, urine output, dialysis or other fluid-tolerance concern. This does not determine whether resuscitation is needed; it prevents a generic crystalloid link when the context has not been individualized.

fields.label: Current perfusion response?
fields.help: Use a documented response after the current intervention. Persistent or worse status requires reassessment of perfusion, source, fluid responsiveness and escalation; it does not automatically authorize another fluid bolus or make a lactate a volume target.

fields.label: Anatomic source-control status?
fields.help: Source control means a reviewed anatomic target that requires a procedure, removal, drainage, debridement or other intervention. “No target identified” is not proof that infection is absent; keep investigating when the clinical context requires it.

fields.label: Microbiology result review?
fields.help: Obtaining cultures is different from reviewing final results. Pending or missing results never count as negative. Review source, response and sampling limitations before narrowing or stopping therapy.

fields.label: Clinician-reviewed septic-shock course?
fields.help: Confirm septic shock clinically, separately from possible infection with hypoperfusion. Acute resuscitation continues while vasopressors are escalating or remain high, or further volume expansion is needed. “Completed” requires these needs to have resolved; an improving lactate alone is insufficient.

quickReference.summary: Make infection likelihood, organ dysfunction, shock and actual antimicrobial status visible; collect cultures/lactate without delaying time-critical care; use the SSC timing branch only when its clinical context is actually entered; then reassess every active intervention and source-control need.
recognition: Sepsis-3: life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection; acute SOFA increase of 2 or more is its clinical operationalization, not a calculation performed here.

Septic shock is a sepsis subset with persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP at least 65 mm Hg and lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate volume resuscitation; this form does not diagnose it.
Do not use qSOFA as a diagnostic gate. SSC 2026 recommends NEWS/NEWS2/MEWS or SIRS over qSOFA as a single in-hospital screen and treats sepsis as a clinical diagnosis.
redFlags: Life-threatening hypotension/hypoperfusion, altered mentation, mottling, cyanosis/decreased oxygenation, worsening organ dysfunction or a rapidly deteriorating trajectory.
Possible/probable/definite septic shock; probable/definite sepsis with organ dysfunction; a source that requires urgent control.
Persistent hypoperfusion after initial treatment, escalating vasopressor need, congestion/renal-cardiac fluid risk or an unknown active resuscitation record.

steps.text: Assess infectious likelihood, acute infection-related organ dysfunction and shock separately. Emergency resuscitation is not gated by qSOFA, cultures or a completed form.
For possible/probable/definite sepsis or septic shock, obtain cultures as soon as possible, ideally before antimicrobials, and measure lactate; do not create a treatment delay.

Reconcile whether a first dose has already been given. Possible/probable/definite septic shock and probable/definite sepsis: immediate, ideally within 1 hour if not already given. Possible sepsis without shock: rapid assessment, then within 3 hours if concern persists. Low likelihood with shock assessed absent: defer while monitoring.

For sepsis-induced hypoperfusion/septic shock, SSC suggests at least 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid in 3 hours with individualization and frequent reassessment. Use actual weight, or consider adjusted/ideal weight if BMI >30. Balanced crystalloids are generally preferred; use saline with traumatic brain injury. Prefer crystalloids alone over routine albumin; large previous crystalloid volumes or cirrhosis may justify albumin, but avoid it with traumatic brain injury. After 30 mL/kg with persistent hypoperfusion, individualize a liberal or restrictive strategy using dynamic response and fluid tolerance.

Initial MAP: generally 65 mm Hg; consider 60–65 at age ≥65. Norepinephrine is first line; unstable shock may need fluids and pressors concurrently. Peripheral initiation can prevent central-access delay. Choose arterial monitoring for high/escalating or multiple pressors, frequent arterial sampling or unreliable cuff readings rather than automatically for every pressor recipient.

Review source, organism-specific resistance risks and local susceptibility. Empiric antifungals are generally discouraged; consider selected high-risk patients individually. Include anaerobic coverage for relevant source risks or other required spectrum. For beta-lactams, prolonged maintenance infusion after the loading dose is strongly recommended; pharmacy must verify the exact regimen.

Narrow or stop unnecessary coverage using confirmed pathogens and susceptibilities (strong recommendation), or review de-escalation when final cultures identify no pathogen (conditional). Pending is not negative. Prefer shorter courses with adequate source control; procalcitonin plus clinical assessment may help stopping when duration is unclear.

IV corticosteroids are suggested for adult septic shock; SSC does not mandate a cortisol result or a fixed pressor threshold. After acute resuscitation ends, consider active fluid removal based on cardiorespiratory status, pressor dose, edema, weight and balance. Improving perfusion alone does not establish readiness. Diuretics or specialist extracorporeal removal require individual indications.
Trend the clinically relevant perfusion response, lactate/CRT when applicable, congestion and source control. When a source requires control, seek early action, ideally within 6 hours.

monitoring: For sepsis/septic shock, SSC quick guidance calls for immediate, ongoing, at least hourly blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate and consciousness monitoring.
Use serial lactate for elevated lactate or septic shock and capillary refill as an adjunct; do not use lactate normalization as a reason to continue unbounded fluid.

Document current fluids, vasopressors, timing, haemodynamic response, fluid balance/congestion, culture timing/results, source-control status and antimicrobial review/de-escalation ownership in the active clinical record.

Review nutrition, glucose, VTE and stress-ulcer prophylaxis with the relevant ICU protocols. Discuss goals of care early; reconcile medicines and communicate treatment, follow-up and rehabilitation needs at transfers and discharge. Dedicated organ-support pathways and the full SSC guideline cover care beyond this compact module.

guides.title: New Inpatient Fever
guides.guideVersion: SCCM/IDSA new fever guideline (2023; adult ICU), NICE CG151, CDC/NIOSH heat guidance, CMAJ serotonin-toxicity review, and DailyMed acetaminophen label, as recorded in the prototype review
guides.resourceNotice: Internal hospital resource tables are omitted from this shared edition.
guides.scope: Adult ICU fever evaluation; special-risk routes are separately source-scoped.
reviewLimitations: SCCM/IDSA directly covers new fever after ICU admission in adult ICU patients without severe immunocompromise. It does not create a general-ward fever bundle, and its recommendations are largely weak or best-practice statements.

The engine deliberately separates SCCM/IDSA’s single 38.3°C ICU definition from the 38.0°C sustained-for-one-hour chemotherapy-neutropenia definition cited in its text. Neither a lower temperature nor an unverified temperature rules out infection or deterioration.

NICE CG151 is an official but older 2012 anticancer-treatment guideline; its 2019 surveillance decision found no evidence requiring an update. It supplies the emergency neutropenic-sepsis route, not a local antimicrobial regimen, dose, or Taiwan formulary recommendation.

The heat branch uses CDC/NIOSH heat-exposure guidance for emergency recognition/cooling only. A separate focused CMAJ serotonin-toxicity review supports recognition-only escalation for drug/toxin concern; neither branch diagnoses a toxic syndrome or provides syndrome-specific treatment.

The conditional IV acetaminophen amounts come from a 2025 DailyMed injection label. They are not a reconciled local regimen or automatic local-vial selection; verify product compatibility, weight, route, all-source exposure, organ/volume risk, allergy, local policy and prescribing authority.
Regimen alignment and live orderability are separate reviews.
This data engine does not write a culture, medication, source-control, precaution, chart or order state.

entry.title: Adult inpatient fever review · ICU reference threshold ≥38.3°C.
entry.scope: ICU-specific testing is labelled and gated to that setting. Lower or unverified temperature does not exclude infection or deterioration.

fields.label: Temperature evidence
fields.help: SCCM/IDSA uses one measured temperature of 38.3°C or higher for its adult ICU fever definition. It prefers central measurement when accuracy is critical; otherwise oral or rectal over axillary, tympanic, or temporal measurement. The 38.0 to <38.3°C sustained-for-one-hour option is the chemotherapy-neutropenia definition cited in that guideline, not its general ICU threshold.

fields.label: Care setting
fields.help: The SCCM/IDSA fever recommendations directly cover adults with new fever after ICU admission, without severe immunocompromise. “Other inpatient area” keeps ICU-specific tests from becoming a ward default.

fields.label: Acute deterioration?
options: Yes — instability, organ or mental change
fields.essential: New instability, respiratory compromise, altered consciousness or organ dysfunction takes priority over the temperature.

fields.label: Anticancer / severe immune risk?
options: Current/recent anticancer therapy or known neutropenia
fields.help: This is a special-population screen, not a diagnosis. NICE says to suspect neutropenic sepsis when a person having anticancer treatment becomes unwell; WBC alone is not a measured ANC. SCCM/IDSA does not directly address transplant or other severe immunocompromise.

fields.label: Heat-hyperthermia emergency?
options: No heat/exertion or drug/toxin emergency — reviewed
Heat/exertion + marked heat or CNS change
Drug/toxin + rigidity, clonus, autonomic or mental change
fields.help: This is an emergency-recognition screen. It does not diagnose serotonin syndrome, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, malignant hyperthermia, or another toxic syndrome, and it does not choose a syndrome-specific regimen.

fields.label: Context after bedside assessment
options: No focus after history and exam
Line, device, wound, or recent surgery
fields.help: Choose the clinical context, not a test bundle. SCCM/IDSA says history and examination should focus subsequent diagnostics; an immediately postoperative, clearly noninfectious temperature may not need an infection investigation.

fields.label: Episode phase
fields.help: This describes the documented clinical trajectory. It is not a culture result, medication-administration record, or authorization to change therapy.

fields.label: Comfort medication status
options: Comfort requested; weight, route, exposure and risk checked
Comfort requested; exposure or risk unresolved
fields.help: “Ready” requires a documented indication, the route and current weight, all oral/IV/rectal and combination-product acetaminophen exposure in the last 24 hours, and liver, renal, volume, and allergy review. It does not select a local product or order.

quickReference.summary: Confirm measured temperature, exclude deterioration/special immune risk/hyperthermia emergency, then target the evaluation and record reassessment.
recognition: SCCM/IDSA defines adult ICU fever as one measured temperature of 38.3°C or higher; central measurement is preferred when accuracy is critical, otherwise oral or rectal is preferred over peripheral routes.
A 38.0 to <38.3°C temperature sustained for at least 1 hour is the chemotherapy-neutropenia definition cited by SCCM/IDSA, not its general ICU threshold.
A lower or unverified temperature does not exclude infection, acute deterioration, or an anticancer-treatment emergency.
redFlags: Any acute instability, new organ dysfunction, hypoxemia, altered mental status, or other deterioration.
A person having anticancer treatment who becomes unwell: suspect neutropenic sepsis and use the emergency oncology/antimicrobial pathway.
Heat/exertion with very high temperature and CNS change, or drug/toxin exposure with rigidity, clonus, autonomic, or mental-status change: urgent emergency assessment.

steps.text: Document temperature value, route, time and peak. Use a more reliable route when the measurement changes management.
Deterioration, hyperthermia concern, severe immune risk, and possible neutropenic sepsis override a stable fever workup.
Use history, examination and focus to choose imaging/specimens. Do not reflexively order urine, sputum, line, stool, viral, or broad imaging panels.
For ICU comfort treatment only after safety review: conditional IV acetaminophen reference is ≥50 kg 1,000 mg q6h or 650 mg q4h; <50 kg 15 mg/kg q6h or 12.5 mg/kg q4h.
steps.dosingNote: All routes/products: max 4,000 mg/24 h at ≥50 kg; otherwise 75 mg/kg/24 h (max 3,750 mg). Check hepatic, renal, volume and allergy risks; local product/policy still govern.

steps.text: Record trajectory, working source, pending results, response, escalation triggers and an explicit next review; a lower temperature alone does not close an episode.

monitoring: Trend temperature with the same documented route/method when feasible; record antipyretic time and every route/product in the daily exposure total.
Set a patient- and setting-specific reassessment interval. The reviewed ICU source does not provide one universal schedule.
For persistent/recurrent fever, re-evaluate focused findings, results, noninfectious causes and escalation need before repeating broad tests or changing treatment.
